newsitem.title: CHINA: China urges reform of battered textile industry.
newsitem.headline: China urges reform of battered textile industry.

text.p: China is urging its beleaguered textile industry to reform its export quota system and cut production of cotton and silk goods to boost prices, the Business Weekly said on Sunday.

"China should step up reform of the current system of quota distribution so that the manufacturing enterprises... will be able to participate in international competition directly," the newspaper quoted Dong Binggen, general manager of China National Garment Corp as saying.
Although many textile makers were capable of exporting on their own, those targeting restricted U.S. and European markets had to buy export quotas from trading firms, Dong said.
The cost of export rights made Chinese textiles more expensive and meant many companies could not compete on the world market, he said.
Excess production of primary cotton and silk products should be slashed to buoy prices, the newspaper said.

Garment exports from January to August totalled $14.2 billion, a drop of 6.2 percent from the same period in 1995. It said exports of yarn and fabric during the first eight months fell by nearly 20 percent from a year-ago period to $7.3 billion.
China's textile exports totalled $37.7 billion in 1995, accounting for about 28 percent of export earnings.
The textile sector had also been hit by painful market-oriented reforms that aimed to wean state-run firms from their dependence on the central government, a separate article in the newspaper said.
"Large and medium-sized state-owned textile enterprises have not been flexible enough to keep pace with the fast-changing market and continue to produce unmarketable products," it said.
Dong urged textile and garment firms to boost product value by making higher quality goods.
The newspaper said textile makers would have to focus on selling to domestic buyers to stay afloat while Beijing straightened out its trade squabbles with other nations.
"The huge domestic market and a gradual return of the international textile market to free-trade norms make future development of the industry possible," the newspaper said.
In September, the United States announced punitive charges against China's 1996 textile and apparel quotas, citing Chinese textile transshipments in violation of trade agreements.
